item.title: A.I. Election Videos Are Flooding Brazil. Could They Sway the Vote?
item.description:
This is a “deepfake” of Brazil’s former right-wing leader endorsing his son’s presidential campaign, even though he is barred from posting online for trying to stage a coup.

Here is Uncle Sam, in a top hat and lugging a bag of cash, on a Brazilian beach while fighter jets swoop overhead and blast a nearby neighborhood.

And here are the two political rivals locked in a bitter battle for Brazil’s presidency, dancing side by side to a viral TikTok song.

Supported by

Brazil spent years targeting electoral lies on the internet. Now, artificial intelligence is stumping the election authorities and reshaping a high-stakes race.

By Ana Ionova

Ana Ionova, a correspondent in Brazil, has been covering the role of technology on democracy since 2021. She reported from Brasília and Rio de Janeiro.

Videos made with artificial intelligence, ranging from the amusing and absurd to the grim and deceitful, have flooded the Brazilian internet ahead of a high-stakes presidential election on Sunday.

This has turned Latin America’s largest democracy into a real-time laboratory for the electoral use of A.I., offering parallels to the United States, where critical midterm elections approach, and to other nations grappling with the effect of powerful new technologies on political life.

But in Brazil, a chronically online nation of 214 million where disinformation has defined elections for nearly a decade, the deluge of A.I. — made by candidates, strategists and ordinary citizens — has become a stark gauge of the nation’s capacity to police online content.

Online disinformation is already a hallmark of Brazil’s electoral season, but A.I.’s prevalence and advancing sophistication are posing a major new challenge for the Brazilian authorities working to protect the integrity of the country’s vote.

Brazil, which has some of the world’s strictest regulations against electoral falsehoods, has issued equally stringent rules on A.I. use during elections. But these guardrails have remained largely untested until now.

“We made the rules, now we’re watching to see what happens,” said Kássio Nunes Marques, chief justice of Brazil’s electoral court, which oversees the vote.

The Brazilian election is pitting President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist, against Flávio Bolsonaro, a right-wing challenger, in a tight contest for the presidency. It is also the biggest test in the region for an ascendant right, which has won seven straight presidential votes in the past 18 months.

In the race to sway a deeply divided Brazilian public, social media has become a key political battleground. And in Brazil, like elsewhere around the world, A.I. has emerged as a potent tool for spreading political messages and shaping the online conversation.

Or just for plain amusement — as in the memes below.

Brazil’s electoral court bars candidates from using “deepfakes,” synthetic but realistic videos or audio messages, while campaigning. It also requires campaigns to clearly label videos generated by A.I.

“When a voter hears a candidate who has been enhanced through artificial intelligence, are they truly hearing the candidate?” said Justice Nunes Marques. “Something that might appear harmless could, in fact, cause harm to the electoral process.”

Tech companies, including Meta, Google and OpenAI, complying with a court request, provided detailed plans about how they would handle A.I. produced and shared on their platforms.

And, ahead of the elections, the electoral authorities banned companies from allowing chatbots from ranking or recommending politicians, though independent watchdogs have found that some platforms have broken that rule.

The country’s broader social media regulations also require digital platforms to swiftly remove posts by regular users who spread electoral lies, attack democratic institutions or otherwise break Brazilian laws.

But the rules haven’t been fine-tuned to distinguish A.I.-generated content meant to mislead from A.I. used for creative expression, according to André Giacchetta, a lawyer who represents social media platforms in Brazil.

“The regulation,” said Mr. Giacchetta, “doesn’t set a threshold for when exactly the use of A.I. begins to constitute potential interference in the electoral process.” This, critics argue, can lead to the overzealous policing of A.I.-generated content that may limit freedom of speech.

To address the new challenges posed by A.I. disinformation, companies like Google and OpenAI have developed ways to flag videos made with their chatbots, such as automatically adding watermarks. Platforms like YouTube are also using biometric identification to catch and remove electoral deepfake videos.

In reality, though, curbing the rapid spread of A.I. falsehoods has been difficult.

If platforms fail to spot and remove deceptive content generated by A.I., the electoral court can and has ordered them to take it down. Yet, experts say that process, sluggish and bureaucratic, is no match for viral A.I. videos that can spread like wildfire across the internet.

“The bad guy we’re now up against is really, really fast,” said Cristina Tardáguila, a disinformation scholar and founder of Agência Lupa, a Brazilian fact-checking agency. Companies are also failing to catch infractions on their own platforms, she added, with a survey by her organization identifying roughly 10 percent of A.I. content created by political candidates was missing a label.

And the sheer volume of content being churned out by bots is making it harder to track A.I. disinformation and its true effects, according to Tai Nalon, head of Aos Fatos, a research group monitoring misinformation in Brazil.

Experts say that the work of policing A.I. is complicated by the way social media platforms have changed. While they once showed users linear timelines of posts, they now rely on highly personalized and secretive algorithms that can aggressively push content onto people’s feeds and widen the reach of A.I. disinformation.

The impartiality of tech companies has also come into question in recent days, after Mr. Lula and independent watchdogs accused Meta of favoring his rival.

At the same time, tech companies have scaled back their moderation efforts, Ms. Nalon added. “We are at a point where the problem has ballooned, while the tools we have on hand are diminished,” she said.

Experts say Brazilians, with their deep love of memes and one of the heaviest social media usage in the world, have been particularly susceptible to the allure of A.I. Some 56 percent of Brazilians say they trust A.I., compared with 40 percent of Americans.

This has made A.I.-generated videos especially effective, and popular, in Brazil.

Seeking to mislead, some of these videos present fake polls or fictitious voters bashing candidates in segments that resemble news reports. Others exaggerate the popularity of each candidate using realistic A.I. videos of fake crowds filling the streets of Brazilian cities.

Jair Bolsonaro, the former right-wing president who is still adored by millions, also features prominently. At a farmer’s market and in front of the presidential palace, an A.I. version of Mr. Bolsonaro has been rallying support for his son, even though he is, in fact, under home confinement as part of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the last election.

The elder Mr. Bolsonaro’s own use of disinformation about election fraud inspired thousands of his supporters to storm Brazil’s capital after his defeat, demanding the military overturn the result.

This time around, many viral election videos have seized on, and amplified, accusations of corruption or fears that the United States may be meddling in the Brazilian elections to help the younger Mr. Bolsonaro.

In one video viewed over 800,000 times, a buff Mr. Lula saves a dog bearing the name of Brazil’s instant payment system, PIX, which the Trump administration has attacked and used to partly justify tariffs.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s supporters, for one, have employed A.I. to cast him as a superhero who will save Brazil by cracking down on crime and kick-starting the economy, while painting his rival as corrupt.

In one video linking Mr. Lula to graft, the president is shown running from the police alongside a Supreme Court justice linked to a corruption scandal hanging over the elections. The crisis in the nation’s top court has damaged Mr. Lula’s image among some voters.

In a different video, the imprisoned banker at the center of that corruption scandal sheds tears over a photo taken with Mr. Bolsonaro, as the candidate frolics in a tub full of cash. Mr. Bolsonaro is being investigated for raising millions of dollars from the banker, Daniel Vorcaro, to finance a biopic about his father.

(In a nation with a rich history of soap operas, dramatic chronicles told by A.I. fruit have also gained popularity, including one featuring an orange as President Trump and an avocado as Mr. Bolsonaro.)

Ultimately, scholars say, A.I. has simply made it faster, cheaper and easier to create misleading or false political narratives that were already circulating online.

And beyond the proliferation of disinformation on the internet, A.I. also holds a different, perhaps more powerful, kind of sway. The popular chatbots dishing out personalized advice to millions of people each day can easily influence political decisions, according to Luiz Alexandre Reali Costa, who runs the Brazilian Observatory for Artificial Intelligence.

“No problem that A.I. brings is totally new,” said Mr. Costa. “But it multiplies the challenges that we already faced.”

Videos at the top of this article by Brazil’s Liberal Party, @filmeiroSource and @iamsmoother via Instagram.

Reporting was contributed by Thayz Guimarães from Brasília, and by Leonardo Coelho, Isabela Cruz and Lis Moriconi from Rio de Janeiro. Additional work by Gray Beltran.

item.title: Who Is Stephen James Hubbard, the American Released by Russia?
item.description:
Russia on Wednesday released a 74-year-old American teacher after holding him as a prisoner for more than four years. He had been convicted of working for Ukraine as a mercenary, charges that the United States said were fabricated.

The teacher, Stephen James Hubbard, was the only American in Russia considered “wrongfully detained” by the State Department and the only one to have been captured in Ukraine during the war and taken to Russia. His release came after President Trump, who has been easing American sanctions on Moscow, appealed directly to Russia’s president, Vladimir V. Putin.

Here’s how Mr. Hubbard became an unlikely pawn in an international conflict.

Mr. Hubbard grew up in Big Rapids, a small Michigan city, with his mother and sister. As a young man, he enlisted in the Air Force and then the National Guard but did not stay long in either. His first marriage, at 20, fell apart, and his second marriage took him to Japan in the mid-1980s. There, he joined the Russian Orthodox Church. He became sympathetic toward Russia.

After his second marriage ended, Mr. Hubbard moved to Cyprus, where a son from his first marriage lived and where he fell in love with a Ukrainian woman. The couple moved to Izium, in eastern Ukraine, in 2014, where Mr. Hubbard taught English online.

Mr. Hubbard was a solitary man, family members said. He avoided email and social media, and he was suspicious of potential government surveillance. When Russia invaded Ukraine, Mr. Hubbard sent family members updates about his daily activities, which included searching for food and going to church. In text messages with a son of his who lives in Japan, he gave no indication that he had joined the Ukrainian military.

Russian forces captured Mr. Hubbard, then 70, just weeks after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022.

The circumstances of his arrest are murky, but the Russian authorities said that Mr. Hubbard had been arrested at the home of an acquaintance and that he had been manning a military checkpoint. The Russian authorities said that Mr. Hubbard had joined a regional territorial unit to defend Ukraine and that he received training, weapons, ammunition and $1,000 a month.

In October 2024, a Moscow court sentenced Mr. Hubbard to six years and 10 months in a penal colony on charges of serving as a mercenary in Ukraine. Russian state news agencies reported that he had pleaded guilty to the charges.

Mr. Hubbard was first held at a detention camp near the Russia-Ukraine border and later imprisoned in at least five different Russian detention centers. At times, his family had no idea where he was and the United States Embassy had no access to him. The New York Times pieced together accounts from fellow prisoners of war to trace where he had been held.

Unlike other Americans held in the Russian prison system, Mr. Hubbard, who spoke neither Ukrainian nor Russian, was kept in the general population, his lawyers said. Ukrainian prisoners of war who were held with Mr. Hubbard said that he had been repeatedly tortured because he was an American — beaten, forced to stand all day, given little food and poor medical care.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

In May 2025, Mr. Hubbard was allowed to call his son in Cyprus, Joseph Coleman. In an interview, Mr. Coleman said that he had spoken for about a minute with his father, who initially sounded like he was in good spirits.

“But then somewhere in the middle it turned and you could you could hear the frustration in his voice,” Mr. Coleman recalled. “You could hear maybe a slight lack of hope.”

Mr. Coleman, who is a Greek Orthodox priest, wrote a long letter to Mr. Putin in September, emphasizing his Orthodox faith and pleading for his father’s release.

“My father is not a man of violence,” Mr. Coleman wrote. “He is a teacher and a peace-loving man, and above all he is my father.”

Mr. Putin announced his decision to release Mr. Hubbard during a meeting with Mr. Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, in St. Petersburg, Russia, on Wednesday.

Russia released Mr. Hubbard unilaterally, rather than in a prisoner swap — suggesting that for Mr. Putin, the American prisoner’s value had changed from a pawn in negotiations to a symbol of his renewed relationship with Mr. Trump.

In the days before Mr. Hubbard’s release, relations between the White House and Ukraine had frayed, with Mr. Trump moving to buy Russian diesel, lifting sanctions on Moscow and pressuring Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries.

Mr. Hubbard, who is in fragile health, will be flown to a State Department facility in Texas for evaluation and treatment. His sister planned to travel to Texas to meet him. Mr. Coleman and another of Mr. Hubbard’s sons, the one who lives in Japan, also flew to the United States to be with their father.

item.title: Australian Politicians Were Already on Edge Before One of Their Own Was Attacked
item.description:
Helen Haines, an independent lawmaker, was still in critical condition after being struck by a vehicle in what the police called a “targeted” attack, when the comments appeared on fellow female politicians’ social media pages.

“What a shame you weren’t there,” one person wrote on the page of Georgie Purcell, a state legislator whose district overlaps with Ms. Haines’s electorate. “She deserves to meet a Land Cruiser,” another wrote in response to an unrelated post by Tanya Plibersek, the minister of social services, in a specific reference to the model of the car that drove into Ms. Haines.

Much remains unknown on Wednesday about the incident two days earlier that shocked the country, when a driver plowed into Ms. Haines outside her electoral office in Wangaratta, in a rural corner of the state of Victoria, leaving her with serious injuries.

Even so, politicians across the ideological spectrum, law enforcement and commentators said it seemed inevitable in the increasingly polarized climate, in which charged language and tirades bordering on threats had become the norm.

A 43-year-old man from Ms. Haines’s district, Brendan Nugent, appeared in court on Wednesday, facing charges of dangerous driving, causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. The police said additional charges could still be brought as the investigation continued, and that they believed the incident was a “deliberate but isolated act.”

Phil Haines, Ms. Haines’s husband of 40 years, said on Wednesday that surgeons had been forced to amputate both of her legs. Ms. Haines was standing behind the trunk of her own vehicle when she was struck, officials said.

“The good news in all of this is Helen is alive, and she’s stable,” Mr. Haines said of his wife, a former nurse who had welcomed new grandchildren in recent months.

“Helen’s road to recovery will be long and difficult, but she is a fighter,” he said, his voice breaking by the end. “She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover.”

Krissy Barrett, commissioner of the Australian Federal Police, said on Wednesday that investigators were still working to determine the motive behind the attack. Nevertheless, the attack “is what many had been dreading for some time,” she said in a news briefing.

“Commonwealth parliamentarians have become increasingly worried about threats directed at them and at their staff,” Ms. Barrett said, adding that investigators with the federal police were charging “almost one individual every week” for targeting members of Parliament or high officeholders.

The sense of threat was further heightened on Wednesday afternoon, when the police in Western Australia, on the other side of the country, arrested a man on suspicion of making verbal threats at an electoral office in Perth while carrying what appeared to be nunchucks.

The police did not say whose office it was, but they said it was on Albany Highway in Victoria Park.

Hannah Beazley, a state representative for Victoria Park, whose office is on that street, said in a statement to local media that a member of the public had entered her office armed with a weapon, and that her staff was “shaken and upset.” There were no injuries, according to the police.

Many politicians said the new environment was threatening Australia’s cherished, down-home style of democracy, where constituents could easily approach their representatives at football matches, community events and local shops, without the throngs of security that shadow high-level officials in places like Britain or the United States.

Australian politics have seen tensions ratcheted up as a far-right party, One Nation, surged to unprecedented levels of support, disrupting a longstanding status quo of the two established parties. The fragmentation has meant increasingly no-holds-barred commentary on topics like immigration, religion and events in the Middle East, amplified by the explosive reach of social media platforms that can fuel the most extreme arguments.

Anne Aly, the minister for small business, said she had received 19 death threats on social media after another lawmaker, Angie Bell, said Ms. Aly should be “shamed and stoned in the square” for a decision over credit card payments to the tax office. Ms. Bell subsequently withdrew her statement, which she made last week during a speech in Parliament.

Ms. Plibersek, who has been in elected office since 1998, said threats had always been part of life in the public eye, but that they had increased in recent years.

“I couldn’t even count the number of death threats, rape threats that I’ve had over the years, including ones that have ended up in court,” she said in an interview with the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. “The thing that’s changed most is the industrial scale of that abuse now. And there’s always been abuse, but I am shocked by the tenor of it.”

David Pocock, an independent senator, said this week that his family had to move homes because of security concerns.

“I think we do need to acknowledge that much of the anger, the division, the at times incredibly hateful comments that have festered in this age of anonymous social media accounts, has spilled over into the real world,” he said on Wednesday in a speech before the National Press Club.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Wednesday that his female colleagues seemed particularly shaken by the attack on Ms. Haines. There had already been an increase in funding for security for members of Parliament in recent years, he said.

“We all have to recognize that politics has got more aggressive,” Mr. Albanese said in a radio interview. “I think the particular impact on women in politics, I think, have got a different form of vilification and aggression toward them.”

item.title: Market Drone Strike Kills at Least 150 as Sudanese Fighters Hit Civilians
item.description:
The drone attack struck a market without warning, sparking an inferno and sending oily smoke skyward. Those who could, scrambled to escape the heat. Many others stood no chance.

The attack on Monday on Amiet market in Abyei, a region disputed between Sudan and South Sudan and contested by the factions in Sudan’s civil war, caused particular shock because it hit a civilian area, rather than a military target.

More than 150 people were killed and the toll was likely to rise, according to Yohana Akol Ngor, the current minister of information in Abyei. Local officials in Abyei blamed the Sudanese military for the attack, which South Sudan’s government condemned, summoning Sudan’s ambassador to the capital, Juba. The Sudanese military was yet to comment on the attack on its social media platforms.

On Tuesday, fires still burned. Video footage showed that parts of the market had been burned to their foundations. Trucks had been stopped in their tracks by the blast, their tires melted.

The strike, which took place when the market was busy and far from the front lines, was further evidence that Sudan’s civil war has — like Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and conflicts within the Democratic Republic of Congo and between Ethiopia and Eritrea — has become dominated by drones.

Easier to procure and operate than conventional airstrikes, drones have allowed armed groups to hit their enemies across vast distances, and both Sudan’s armed forces and the paramilitary it is fighting against have shown a disregard for civilian life. Hundreds of people have been killed in drone strikes this month alone, according to witnesses, humanitarian organizations and media reports, though precise numbers are difficult to determine.

Abyei is an oil-rich province claimed both by South Sudan, a nation born in 2011 after decades of civil war, and by the Sudanese government, itself now trapped in another devastating conflict.

Since the fighting erupted in April 2023, between Sudan’s military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, around 14 million people — more than a quarter of the country’s population — have been forced to flee their homes. The country’s health ministry puts the civilian death toll at more than 11,000, but some estimates are as high as 400,000 killed.

In one brazen attack, the R.S.F. attacked Port Sudan over successive days in May 2025, hitting the city’s airport and a hospital. The strikes, which the paramilitary said were on military targets, demonstrated the group’s ability to project drones across hundreds of miles of open territory, a significant display of force that showed that nowhere in the country was safe.

Drones are less costly than other weapons and do not require a large expenditure of resources. They allow the combatants to put pressure on civilian areas as the war has reached an effective stalemate, according to Andreas Krieg, a Middle East expert at King’s College London.

The United Arab Emirates has constructed an economic supply chain that enabled the R.S.F. to source drones from China, while the S.A.F. had access to both Iranian and Turkish drones, he said. The Emirates denies it backs either side in the war.

“The drones aren’t cheap,” he said, but “in Sudan, going after basic civilian infrastructure is a way of putting pressure on the civilian population and therefore ultimately on the combatants.” Despite their toll, the attacks are unlikely to alter the underlying dynamics of the war, he said.

On the ground, the war has settled into what some analysts describe as a de facto partition of the country. The R.S.F. controls Darfur in the west, while the S.A.F. holds sway over the capital, Khartoum, and the east. Parts of Kordofan, a central region that includes the city of El Obeid, are contested, as well as Blue Nile state near the border with Ethiopia.

The recent strikes show that, despite the relative stasis, the threat of the war remains undiminished to civilians across the country.

Dozens of gold workers in northern Sudan were killed earlier this month when warplanes bombed an open air mine near the Egyptian border. Last week, dozens also died in an attack on a market in the town of Nyala, an R.S.F. stronghold.

The United Nations Secretary General, António Guterres, on Tuesday condemned the “relentless drone attacks across Sudan.” He cited an attack in Khartoum that killed three children and other attacks in South Darfur state and White Nile state.

“These attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict,” he said through his spokesman, Stéphane Dujarric.

item.title: ‘People Are So Rude’: Can Britain Shhhh Headphone Dodgers on Trains?
item.description:
Many Londoners would agree that there is a set of unwritten rules for travelers on the city’s Underground and iconic red buses. Eye contact is largely a no-go. Interactions are kept at a minimum, with exceptions for cute babies and dogs.

But in recent years, one long-held convention, that riders should keep their electronic devices quiet, has appeared to be crumbling — in many places around the world — as some travelers scroll videos or play music without headphones.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain this week announced a national campaign against what he described as “one of the most annoying things on public transport.”

The government is urging passengers to use headphones on trains or risk being asked to leave the train or face a fine, and is publicizing existing policies that allow the local authorities to issue fines of up to 100 pounds (about $134) to tackle loud music on buses. The reality of how that will be enforced remains unclear, however.

On Tuesday morning, London commuters weighed in on the plans.

Patricia Foley has lived in London her whole life and said that she always felt that people using public transportation were polite. In recent years, though, she feels that has changed.

“People are so rude now, and I am not sure why,” she said. “And I would never challenge anyone myself.”

She said she was happy about government efforts to address antisocial behavior, as it would take the responsibility off other passengers.

“I think it’s a brilliant proposal because who wants to sit next to someone watching a film or something loud?” she said. “But how do you implement it? They are not going to spend money on people patrolling this.”

Geoff Newnham said that he found music blaring from people’s phones irritating and that he was in favor of the idea of fines “because it gets the message out there.” But he, too, was skeptical it could work.

“I think the reality is that enforcing those fines is going to be very difficult, and it’s probably just going to cause more issues,” he said. “The people that are quite happy to obnoxiously play their music are not going to be the people who will necessarily respond well to being challenged over it.”

He and his partner, Freya Skerten, had spent a long weekend in London with their 11-week-old baby and were waiting to board a train home. Ms. Skerten gently rocked their daughter’s stroller back and forth in an effort to keep her asleep as she explained that most people kept to themselves on public transportation.

“I think it’s a real British thing, isn’t it?” she said, but added with a smile, “Unless you have a baby — then everyone wants to speak to you.”

Ken Oluwadare was quietly scrolling through his phone on his way to university. He is studying for a degree in popular music performance.

“I’m studying drumming and I love music, but it’s only on when I am wearing my headphones,” he said.

In a hushed voice, he said he would prefer to see a campaign for more public awareness rather than fines. “Maybe the way they announce the next stop, they should also be telling people, ‘On this train, we won’t be allowing any loud noises.’”

“I don’t think it’s going to be effective; it’s nonsense,” Emma Hawkins said of the government’s plans. “I’d rather they spend more time dealing with other crime.”

She and her daughter, Bea Hawkins, were waiting for a train in Paddington Station and agreed that noisy neighbors on the bus and train were a real nuisance.

“I think it’s long overdue for someone to do something about this,” Bea said. “Especially when someone is watching Reels, it’s so annoying because it’s this different blast of music every few seconds,” she added, referring to Instagram’s short-form vertical videos.

Tosh Polpitiye, who was waiting on the train platform with his two dogs, Guinness and Ouzo, during the Tuesday rush hour, said he thought fines could have a positive effect on riders’ experience.

“I don’t want to hear other people’s phones,” he said. “I don’t want to hear what they are listening to. I don’t even like it when they have their speakers on to make a call.” He added, “You aren’t in your house.”

The fines could make more people compliant, he said, likening it to penalties for breaking the speed limit: “It’s consequences that typically make people not want to do those actions.”

item.title: Macron Says Trump Does Not Like France and Distorts Its Troubles
item.description:
President Emmanuel Macron of France said on Wednesday that President Trump does not like France and that he was among the leaders who had made false claims about unrest there to advance their own political interests at France’s expense.

When asked whether Mr. Trump does not like France, Mr. Macron, addressing a group of reporters, said: “Well, one has to admit it. All the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t like our country.”

Political leaders on both sides of the Atlantic “who echo what certain circles obviously want people to believe about what happened in France, they’re campaigning at our expense,” he said.

The worst rioting in years shook France over the weekend, spinning off from demonstrations about public education and the rising cost of living. Several government buildings were attacked and some were set on fire, nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, and more than 3,000 shops were looted or damaged, leading to the arrest of more than 2,500 people across France, officials said.

At a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, two weeks before midterm U.S. elections, Mr. Trump said, “If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France, a once great nation that is being conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity.”

France’s government has accused “ultraleft militants” and opportunistic looters of causing the violence. The far-right, anti-immigration party, the National Rally, has also accused the far left, which it said formed an alliance with “predators from the suburbs.” In France, “the suburbs” usually refers to working-class areas with large numbers of immigrants, primarily from Africa, and their descendants.

Several foreign leaders and politicians, including President Trump and Vice President JD Vance — both of whom have expressed support for the National Rally — amplified its critiques, saying the unrest was caused by immigrants.

The identities of the black-clad and masked rioters captured on footage is unknown. Of the more than 2,500 people arrested, 95 percent were men and 70 percent were adults, according to Gérald Darmanin, France’s justice minister. They included “people from immigrant backgrounds, people who are foreigners, but there are also people who are fully integrated and who are French,” Mr. Darmanin added, without providing further details.

Mr. Macron made his comments on Mr. Trump in Qatar, on a three-day diplomatic trip to the Middle East aimed at securing a steady supply of fuel to lower prices at home. He has been trying to address one of the demonstrators’ main complaints, high living expenses, as the government seeks to reassert its authority after the rioting.

“There are people who claimed that we had been overrun by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Mr. Macron said. When reporters asked if this included Mr. Trump, he replied, “among others.”

“You know, at times like these, you can see who likes France and who doesn’t,” he said.

With just seven months until his decade in office ends, Mr. Macron, who is term-limited, has failed to solve problems afflicting France’s economy and welfare system.

He now faces a systemic crisis, with a rising far right, a looming financial crisis and nationwide protests. Combined with a deadlocked Parliament, the government, which failed to pass the national budget on time for two years running, does not seem poised to overcome the crisis.

Mr. Macron said on Wednesday that the government was following a “clear road map” to restore order and address the demands of protesters, particularly high school students. On Thursday, he said, he would attend a meeting with intelligence agencies, the prime minister and some cabinet ministers to receive a detailed briefing on how the unrest was handled.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu met Wednesday with labor union leaders who have encouraged the protests. The discussion was inconclusive, according to Sophie Binet, the leader of a major union, who said nothing concrete was put on the table.

“The time has come to take the mobilization to the next level: The strike must take over,” she told journalists after the meeting.

Though France’s main unions are focusing on a day of protests and strikes scheduled for Nov. 5, some protesters and student leaders have called for more demonstrations this weekend. Fabien Roussel, the head of France’s Communist Party, said his supporters would join authorized demonstrations on Saturday. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the head of the far-left party France Unbowed, called on his followers to join protests to “help the young people march peacefully.”

The Interior Ministry said the police and gendarmerie staff would be bolstered on Saturday, with elite units of each deployed as well as military troops.

Curfews and restrictions on gatherings have been imposed in parts of several French cities most affected by the unrest this week. In Paris, a curfew and a ban on unauthorized gathering in parts of the city was extended to Thursday morning, the police said on Wednesday. Other cities, like Marseille, have decided that restrictions will remain in place until Friday.

item.title: Why Palestinians Hope Israelis Will Oust Netanyahu in Pivotal Election
item.description:
Israelis have described the election to be held on Oct. 27 as the most important in their history. For Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the stakes are just as high — even though they do not have a vote.

In previous elections, Palestinians tended to dismiss the candidates to be Israel’s leader as a choice between bad and worse. This time, in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, ignited the devastating war in Gaza, many say that replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is imperative.

“These elections are existential,” said Nidal Kuhail, 32, a Palestinian who lives in a 6-by-4 meter tent with his three sisters and parents in Gaza after being displaced by the war. “It’s now become a matter of to be or not to be.”

Mr. Netanyahu has vowed to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state, and his government has built Israeli settlements in the West Bank at a breakneck pace.

Gadi Eisenkot, Mr. Netanyahu’s main opponent, has also rejected Palestinian statehood. But he has promised to curb settler violence in the West Bank and engage with the Trump administration’s cease-fire plan to rebuild Gaza.

The split is one reason Palestinians are paying particular attention to this election, even though their plight is not a major election topic for Israelis in the campaign. In interviews with Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank, they have made clear they do not expect Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents to radically change things for the better. But they are desperate to avoid another four years of Mr. Netanyahu, whose government — the most right-wing since Israel was established in 1948 — has made life almost unbearable.

In Gaza, the Israeli government has waged a relentless bombing campaign even after reaching a cease-fire with Hamas just over a year ago. Israeli strikes since then have killed more than 1,400 people, according to local health officials, and Israel has expanded the area of Gaza it controls. The Israeli military says it is targeting Hamas militants and protecting nearby communities in Israel.

In the West Bank, Israeli settlers have built outposts, harassed Palestinians and set homes and mosques ablaze. Settler attacks on Palestinians have escalated there during the annual olive harvest of recent weeks, which is a cultural touchstone for Palestinians and an economic lifeline for many families. On Monday, the Israeli police said they had detained at least 10 Israelis after settlers assaulted Palestinians, along with an American press photographer and European diplomats, during the olive harvest. But the government has largely done little to quell the violence, analysts and rights groups say.

Mr. Netanyahu has occasionally denounced the extremist attackers, but the assaults have continued. He recently hailed the establishment of more than 100 new settlements in the West Bank and pledged that “more were on the way” as part of an effort to entrench Israeli rule across the territory.

“This government made a massive effort to realize this generations-old dream,” he told a conference of settlers in August. In the decades since Israel occupied the West Bank in 1967, hundreds of thousands of Israelis have moved there and established communities, widely known as settlements, that are broadly considered illegal under international law.

The Israeli government has also waged economic warfare against the Palestinian Authority, which administers major Palestinian cities in the West Bank. Since the Oct. 7 attacks, the Israeli government has largely banned Palestinians from working in Israel, cutting off a crucial source of income.

The government has also withheld billions of dollars in tax revenue from the Palestinian Authority, after accusing it of using the money to fund terrorism. Palestinian officials deny the accusation.

Mr. Eisenkot has said he broadly supports Israeli settlements. But he has vowed to dismantle any that were built in parts of the West Bank that are supposed to be administered by the Palestinian Authority under the interim peace agreements reached between the Palestine Liberation Organization and Israel in the 1990s.

Spurred by Mr. Netanyahu’s far-right allies, Israel has established new settlements in parts of the northern West Bank where Israelis have not lived in recent years. Settlers have also erected many more outposts that are illegal even under Israeli law.

Israeli extremists residing at the outposts have routinely carried out acts of violence — for instance, stealing livestock and cutting down olive trees — which have forced entire communities to flee. In interviews this month, many Palestinian residents said that they hoped a new Israeli government would curb the violence.

Haitham Abdel Jaber, 47, was hospitalized last week with a head injury after settlers assaulted him. Mr. Abdel Jaber, an American citizen, said on Sunday that he was harvesting olives with relatives near his home in Burqa, a village close to Ramallah, when masked assailants hurled stones at them.

Mr. Abdel Jaber said he was hit by a rock while he and his relatives tried to run away. As he was on the ground, he said, his attackers beat and kicked him before fleeing.

The Israeli military said that it sent troops to the area after a report of “friction” between Israelis and Palestinians, including rock throwing.

“We hope Netanyahu loses in the elections,” Mr. Abdel Jaber said. “It’s not that Eisenkot will work for the sake of the Palestinians, but the situation might get better.”

The Israeli economic restrictions have pushed the Palestinian Authority close to bankruptcy.

Nasser Osaily, an entrepreneur active in real estate and importing, said the authority owes him millions of dollars in reimbursements for business he has done with foreign donors. Business owners that occupy stores in his properties, meantime, were struggling to pay rent because Palestinian consumers had little money to spend in them, he added.

“It’s a policy of strangulation. It’s like being grabbed by the neck,” Mr. Osaily said in his office in Hebron.

Bezalel Smotrich, a settler leader now serving as Israel’s finance minister, has urged the next government to crack down even harder. In a podcast interview this month, he said that Israel should “go to war” in the West Bank and do “what we did in Gaza,” a reference to the military campaign that has razed large parts of the enclave.

Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents stress they would seek stability in the territory. Yoram Cohen, who is a senior member of Mr. Eisenkot’s party and a former Israeli intelligence chief, said this would include clamping down on Israeli extremists who attack Palestinians and easing the economic pressure. “We have no interest in igniting a new front,” he said at a party event in Tel Aviv this month.

Palestinian officials in the West Bank, who generally avoid endorsing Israeli candidates, are openly advocating a change of government.

Ahmed Majdalani, a senior Palestinian official, said there was “a huge difference between Netanyahu and Eisenkot,” adding that he hoped Mr. Eisenkot would release confiscated funds to the Palestinian Authority.

“We’re not even saying ‘let’s establish a state’ at this point. We’re saying ‘let’s solve these problems,’ because this can restore trust between the two of us,” Mr. Majdalani said. “If Netanyahu is re-elected, though, it will be a disaster for us and the Israelis.”

Palestinians in Gaza, living under near-daily bombardment, hope they will gain if Mr. Netanyahu loses.

The prime minister has largely refused to cooperate with President Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza, which has sought to push ahead with a plan to disarm Hamas in exchange for Israel withdrawing from the Palestinian enclave.

Now, senior members of Mr. Netanyahu’s governing coalition say Israel will encourage Gazans to “voluntarily emigrate” en masse if it is returned to power in the elections. Mr. Smotrich, the finance minister, called last month for Israel to keep conditions in Gaza as miserable as possible so as to “take away their hope.”

Palestinians in the enclave are still living in the rubble of damaged or destroyed buildings and tents, which they fear will become permanent homes.

“Life in Gaza has totally stopped as people await the Israeli elections,” said Jaser Abu Mousa, a political analyst from Gaza.

It is unclear what Mr. Eisenkot would do differently, as many Israelis agree the government should maintain tight restrictions on the movement of goods into Gaza and continue airstrikes against Hamas. Mr. Eisenkot’s allies say they will engage more closely with the Board of Peace in an effort to dislodge Hamas.

Saed Abu Aita, 46, has lived with a piece of shrapnel lodged in his chest since early in the war. It occasionally causes a sharp pain, reminding him of the Israeli attack that he said killed his father, Hamed, and two daughters, Mira, 8, and Tala, 13, and left him unconscious.

Mr. Abu Aita and his wife have not been able to visit their graves, which are in the portion of Gaza that Israel controls. The past three years, he said, have been “a catastrophic journey of torture.”

“I’ve lost everything and I can’t get anything,” he added.

The Israeli elections, he said, will not bring a comprehensive solution for Gaza. But he hopes that removing Mr. Netanyahu from power would ease the worst of the daily struggles.

“If the extremists go, perhaps we will be able to return to our homes, get better health care and more humanitarian supplies,” he said.
